cells.tense: The pen is in your hand and it's steady, right here, today.
cells.ask: Put one rule in writing for something that doesn't have one yet — a single line, drafted before you're sure it's right. The drafting shows you what you're actually building.
cells.core:
You decide what gets repeated here, and you do it on purpose. Not by decree — by weighing what's worth keeping and letting the rest drop, and by changing your mind when the thing in front of you asks you to. What you set down holds, and people build on it without being told to. When it's working, the structure carries what it's meant to carry and stays out of the way, and you're free to walk off from it for a while.

There's more pattern available than you've taken pen for. The next piece is small and doesn't have a name yet, and putting it in writing is the part that shows you what you're making — not a plan on paper, just the first thing you're willing to stand behind. You don't have to be sure of it before it goes down.
cells.sheetLine: You choose what becomes the rule, and you're steady with it.
cells.verb: setting down the first piece the rest gets built around
cells.place: where the working rules get decided and everyone lives inside them

cells.tense: You're already laid out in a future where the structure is finished and everyone is in it.
cells.ask: Let one rule you've set stand for a week without tightening it. Watch what the structure does when you're not holding it up.
cells.core:
You know how to make a frame hold. Set the thing down, watch where it bends, adjust — that's a working hand, and it's why what you build tends to stand. Running well, the frame does its job and you're free to leave it alone and do something else with your day.

Lately the building has crowded out the thing it was meant to hold. A plan comes up, a conversation starts, and you're already three steps ahead of what's actually here, laying bricks for rooms nobody has walked into. The tightening keeps you busy in a way that's hard to put down. Letting one rule stand isn't a test of whether you're needed. It's where you find out what the structure does on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're laying bricks ahead of the room. Some of them aren't asking to be laid.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door you walked through already, looking back at how the last structure went.
cells.ask: Describe one thing you run, out loud, in words you'd actually say. Not the plan — the thing itself, as if someone had just asked you what you do.
cells.core:
You can take a mess and give it a shape people can work inside. That's a real hand, and it doesn't need proving. When it's going well, you name the shape and other people pick it up from there without being told twice.

What's happening instead is that you've been building smaller and quieter, in places where nobody can come along and pull it apart. The work is still there. The saying of it went out of the room, and a plain sentence about what you do, spoken where you can hear it, puts the fact back in front of you instead of behind you. Whoever hears it isn't the point; the hearing is.

cells.tense: You're already writing the rules — the pen is down and the lines are appearing, and you're calling it something else.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you already run, then the next line — what you'd tell someone joining tomorrow. Two sentences total.
cells.core:
You're already the one setting the pattern. The order things happen in, what gets repeated, what counts as finished — that's you, and it's been you a while. You describe it as just how it goes, or as nobody's job in particular, and the room runs on it either way. Said out loud, the same thing would sound like someone standing at the front of a room saying 'this is how we do it here,' meaning themselves by it, and nobody would blink.

Two sentences on paper, where you can look at them, puts the fact in your hands instead of leaving it in the room — and paper doesn't argue back.

attempts.check: The record gives me the card (seed of directed form, first commitment to structure), the seat (building the frame others work inside), and the partner's mechanism at each status — it does not give me anything about this person's history, so every cell has to stay at the level of what the capacity is doing in the present. The likeliest objection is that 'you're the one setting the frame' could be heard as praise or as a claim about their whole character; I narrow it to the specific thing — choosing what becomes the pattern — so they can say 'no, someone else set this up' and still have something usable. The ask survives being wrong at every status because each one is a small, watchable act at the table (write the first rule, let a rule stand unrevised, write down one thing they already run, name a rule in their own words), which teaches them something about how the pattern forms whether or not my read of them is right. The sentence that serves me rather than them is any line about 'the frame' as a grand thing — I cut that and keep the plain version: the thing that gets repeated becomes the rule.
